title: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
hookLine: feet on the floor, hands on the knees — you have one

cards: Quick check. Where are your feet right now? If that took a second to answer, no surprise.
A day can be lived about a foot above your own shoulders: in a screen, in a conversation that already happened, in tomorrow's list.
Meanwhile there's a whole body down here, keeping you alive, carrying you around, sending messages that mostly go unopened. Feet on the floor. Hands on the knees.

teach.h: ASANA: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.
teach.b: Start with an old instruction for sitting. The Yoga Sutras, compiled in India and traditionally credited to Patanjali, say almost nothing about the poses people now call yoga.
On posture they're very brief: the seat should be steady and easy. The word is asana, and there it means simply a seat, the place you sit. Steady, so you're not fidgeting.

One of the oldest Buddhist teachings on mindfulness puts the body first too: breathing in, breathing out, standing, walking, sitting, lying down. Knowing, plainly, what the body is doing while it's doing it.
Then, in 1890, William James turned common sense around. Common sense says we cry because we're sad.
James said it may run the other way: "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." Psychologists have argued about how far that goes ever since.
The smaller point is one you can check for yourself: body and feeling are tangled together, and a change in one tends to show up in the other. That's why the body makes such a good doorway.
You can't always choose your thoughts.
You can usually choose to put your feet flat on the floor.

how: Yoga, Zen and many Buddhist and Christian contemplative practices begin by settling the body: a steady, comfortable seat, feet grounded, hands at rest, with attention on how the body feels.

practice: Here's the practice. Before the bell, set your feet flat on the floor if you can, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap.
For about forty-five seconds, feel three things in turn: your feet, whatever is holding you up, and your hands, just resting. Steady and easy. That's the whole seat.

wordCard.voice: Body. Where mindfulness starts, and a place you can always come back to. Ninth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, asana: a seat. Yoga Sutra 2.46 asks that it be sthira and sukha, steady and easy.

carryVoice: Your line: come back down. Your feet are always somewhere to land. See you tomorrow.
